Dose Trajectories of Modern Antipsychotic Programs in Schizophrenia (2009–2026)

Jerry Hu

2026-08-13

← PK/PD Home Page

1 Summary

Background. Dose selection for a Phase 2 study in a CNS indication — and whether to dose flexibly — is a recurring design decision with sparse prospective evidence. This study reconstructs how completed antipsychotic programs actually chose, tested and revised their doses. For six schizophrenia programs, it traces the tested and recommended dose and schedule from first-in-human through post-marketing, and identifies what data drove each change.

Methods. The cohort was defined by rule: every new molecular entity oral antipsychotic FDA-approved for schizophrenia from 2009 onward (8 programs). Six were reconstructed in full. Four met a pre-specified criterion of a dose-related regulatory action or post-approval dose revision (iloperidone, lurasidone, cariprazine, lumateperone); two were chosen as contrasts (ulotaront, a flexible-dose Phase 2 success that failed in fixed-dose Phase 3; xanomeline–trospium, whose label transcribes its titration trial design). Every study and every dose or schedule change was extracted from FDA approval packages, archived labels and publications; each fact carries its source and whether the primary document was read in full. Each study was classified by the dose-related question it was run to answer, and each post-approval label change by the question it resolved. Receptor occupancy was annotated against the 65–80% striatal D2 window.

Results. The extraction covers 329 studies and 93 dose or schedule changes, from 146 sources (88% primary documents read in full). Of the 5 approved programs, 4 lowered a wide early ceiling to a narrow registered range, each for a different reason. Iloperidone was capped by QT prolongation under forced titration. Lurasidone took a conservative cap that was later doubled (80 to 160 mg/day (approved 2012-04-26, ~18 months post-launch)). Cariprazine was capped by its metabolite below the demonstrated efficacy range (6 mg/day cap despite efficacy shown at doses up to 9 mg/day). Lumateperone was approved at a single dose well below the D2 window (39% peak D2 occupancy at the approved 42 mg dose). The two novel-mechanism programs had no occupancy anchor at all. Ulotaront’s Phase 3 failure followed a Phase 2 that never explored the upper end of its range (DIAMOND 2 tested a fixed 100 mg/day never given in Phase 2). Across the 194 studies of the six programs, 35 were run to find out who needs a different dose (drug interactions, organ impairment, special populations) and 13 to characterise the dose-response relationship. After approval, only 1 of 25 label changes moved the approved dose range.

Conclusions. In this cohort, flexible dosing in Phase 2 repeatedly deferred — rather than answered — the dose-response question, and regulators either imposed fixed-dose designs (lurasidone), demanded high-dose safety data (iloperidone), or accepted titration schemes transcribed from flexible-dose trials (xanomeline–trospium). Where titration was obligatory or was itself the intended label, the flexible design was the right instrument; the failure mode is its use as a substitute for dose-finding, since a flexible trial estimates a titration strategy and not the shape of the dose-response curve. Doses left untested in Phase 2 proved close to unrecoverable afterwards. The occupancy playbook that guided the D2 era did not transfer to the newest mechanisms, which leaves fixed-dose Phase 2 dose-ranging as the only remaining place the question can be settled.

2 Background

A standard interview question in clinical pharmacology asks: what are the considerations for dose selection of a Phase 2 study in a central nervous system (CNS) indication — specifically, flexible dosing? The textbook answer lists dose-response characterization, tolerability-driven titration, and the risk that flexible designs confound dose with patient state. This study asks what the completed record actually shows.

2.1 What “the dose-response question” means here

The phrase compresses five distinct questions, which a development programme answers with different designs and at different costs:

  1. Is there a relationship at all over the range that can be given — or is the drug flat because the tested range already sits on a plateau, or wholly below threshold?
  2. What is the shape — where the curve rises, where it bends, and whether the top of the tested range is on the flat part. Near-maximal effective doses (ED95) are answers to this question.
  3. What is the safety and tolerability curve over the same range. This one is generally monotone increasing, so the object of interest is the joint behaviour of curves 2 and 3 — the vertical gap between them.
  4. Which dose, and how wide a range, goes into confirmatory trials and onto the label. A decision derived from 2 and 3, not a separate estimand.
  5. Is the optimum individual or population-level — does a patient failing at one dose benefit at a higher one, and can that patient be identified prospectively? Titration presumes yes to both.

Question 5 is decisive and rarely examined. Flexible dosing is only rational if individual optima genuinely differ and the treating clinician can detect who needs more. In acute schizophrenia, with a four-to-six-week symptom scale as the readout and no pharmacodynamic biomarker at the bedside, the up-titration decision is made on early non-response — a weak predictor of eventual response.

Four dosing designs appear in the studies below, and the distinction between them matters for reading everything that follows. Fixed-dose: each arm is randomised to one dose held constant. Flexible-dose: the clinician adjusts the dose within a range on response and tolerability, so the dose a patient ends on is not randomised. Forced titration: every patient climbs a fixed schedule to a fixed target — a design in which schedule and dose are one thing. Forced titration with an optional top step (the xanomeline–trospium trials) is coded as flexible in the tables below, because the top dose is reached by a tolerability decision rather than by design. In addition, Phase 1 dose escalation and single-dose studies are named as such.

A flexible-dose trial delivers a clean randomised estimate of exactly one thing: the effect of a titration strategy — start here, escalate by these rules — versus control. That is a legitimate estimand, and it is the right one when the label will itself be a titration. What such a trial cannot deliver is the shape of the dose-response curve, for three structural reasons:

  • Dose is determined by the patient’s response. The dose a patient ends on is caused by their response and tolerability: non-responders are pushed up, responders stay low. The observed dose–outcome association is confounded by prognosis and can come out flat, or inverted, regardless of the truth. Because nothing was randomised to dose, no valid contrast exists to be recovered by adjustment.
  • Dose is confounded with time. Higher doses occur later, and so do placebo response, spontaneous improvement, and differential dropout.
  • The top of the range is estimated on a selected minority — the patients tolerant enough to climb — or, as one program in this cohort shows, is never reached at all.

Exposure–response analysis does not repair this when the spread in exposure is generated by titration decisions rather than by pharmacokinetic variability at a fixed dose: exposure then inherits the same dependence on response that dose has. It does retain some value where patients are held at the same step and differ in exposure only through clearance, food or adherence — which is why regulators have accepted such analyses in forced-titration programs. The distinction is applied below to the one program in the cohort that argued its dose case on exposure–response grounds.

2.2 Why antipsychotics

Antipsychotics in schizophrenia are a favorable class for this question. The pharmacology has a quantitative spine — striatal D2 receptor occupancy of roughly 65–80% has long been treated as the antipsychotic therapeutic window, with extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) rising above it — and the modern programs fall entirely inside the ClinicalTrials.gov era. The window itself was established by PET in the 1990s and has since been examined by dose–occupancy meta-analysis (Farde 1992; Kapur 2000; Siafis 2023). The class also spans the question’s extremes: programs that titrated because they had to, programs capped below their own efficacy data, a single-dose approval at 39% occupancy, and two novel mechanisms (a TAAR1 agonist and an M1/M4 muscarinic agonist) for which no occupancy anchor existed.

Objective. For six antipsychotic development programs in schizophrenia, reconstruct how the tested and recommended dose level and schedule evolved from first-in-human through post-marketing, identify what data — PK and metabolite behavior, receptor occupancy, tolerability, efficacy, regulatory feedback — drove each change (RQ1), and map the dose-related question each subsequent study was designed to answer (RQ2).

A companion study, How much of a dose trajectory does the registry see?, benchmarks how much of these trajectories is recoverable from the ClinicalTrials.gov footprint alone.

3 Methods

3.1 Cohort and reconstruction depth

The cohort rule was fixed before extraction: every new molecular entity (NME) oral antipsychotic FDA-approved for schizophrenia in 2009 or later. Eight programs qualify (table below). The qualifying set was assembled by walking the FDA’s own NME approval listings for 2009 onward and keeping the oral antipsychotics with a schizophrenia indication; each survivor is carried in programs.csv with its NDA number, so the denominator can be checked against Drugs@FDA rather than taken on trust. It is a small enough set to enumerate exhaustively, which is why no search strategy applies to this step. Aripiprazole (2002) predates the rule and is cited only as background for the partial-agonist programs; long-acting injectable line extensions are recorded as single formulation events, not separate programs.

Two depths of reconstruction. Every program below was enumerated the same way — the complete study list from its FDA approval package. Six programs were then reconstructed in full: every dated dose or schedule change, the data behind each change, and the dose question each study answered. The remaining three were left at the study list alone. Depth follows from whether a program has a dose story to reconstruct, not from how much evidence it carries: asenapine contributes the largest study count of any program here and no dose events at all, because its adult-schizophrenia dosing has never changed.

The six fully reconstructed programs are five from the cohort plus one outside it. Four met a pre-specified criterion — (a) a dose-related regulatory action, or (b) a post-approval revision of the originally approved adult-schizophrenia dose or administration: iloperidone (2008 not-approvable letter demanding safety data at 20–24 mg/day), lurasidone (2012 maximum-dose doubling), cariprazine (2013 complete response letter for dose-related late-emerging toxicity), and lumateperone (2021 food-requirement removal; 2022 special-population strengths). Two contrast cases were chosen rather than selected by the criterion, because they illustrate the extremes of the flexible-dosing question: xanomeline–trospium, the index case whose label titration transcribes its trial design, and ulotaront — which is not a member of the eight-program cohort, having been terminated in Phase 3 without ever reaching approval. That two of the six were chosen for what they illustrate is a selection constraint on the discussion, taken up in the Limitations.

The three list-only programs — asenapine, brexpiprazole and olanzapine/samidorphan — received the study enumeration and nothing further. Enumerating them was not incidental: it is what lets the companion recall study’s reference standard cover all eight approved programs rather than the five reconstructed here.

3.2 Data sources and extraction

Facts were extracted into four linked tables (studies; dose and schedule changes; sources; occupancy data), each row keyed to a source with a stated verification level: primary document read in full (FDA review PDFs, archived DailyMed label versions), seen only in search snippets, or secondary. Study enumeration used the FDA approval packages, whose clinical-pharmacology reviews list the complete Phase 1 program and whose medical reviews list all controlled trials; post-approval events come from supplemental approvals and the archived label version history. For ulotaront, which has no FDA package, the registry and publications were used instead. The three list-only programs (asenapine, brexpiprazole, olanzapine/samidorphan) received the same FDA-package study enumeration — without reconstruction of their dose changes — so that the companion recall study’s reference standard covers all eight approved programs. 88% of the 146 sources are primary documents read in full.

Two extraction rules protect the companion registry-recall study: trial registry identifiers were recorded only when stated in an FDA document or publication (never looked up in the registry), and registry content was not used to fill study attributes for the approved programs.

Search and cut-off. All sources were retrieved and verified on 2026-08-13, which is the data cut-off: label changes, approvals or publications after that date are not represented. The FDA stream is an enumeration rather than a search — for each program the complete approval package and the full archived label version history were read end to end, so no query terms apply. The remaining streams were searched rather than enumerated, and are therefore the components where recall is not guaranteed: publications were located from the reference lists of the FDA reviews and by drug-name searches for PET occupancy and dose-response reports; occupancy values were taken from those publications plus two curated meta-analyses fixed in advance (Siafis 2023, Leucht 2020); and ulotaront, which has no FDA package, was reconstructed from its registry records, sponsor announcements and publications. No database was searched systematically with a recorded Boolean query, so the non-FDA streams are best treated as a purposive sample of the public record rather than an exhaustive one.

Each study row carries the dose-related question it was run to answer, assigned from the study’s position and design in the program (RQ2); inserted special studies — positron emission tomography (PET) occupancy, thorough-QT (TQT), food-effect — are read as markers of a question the program needed answered. Numeric total-daily-dose bounds were curated per study from the arm descriptions, excluding comparator arms.

For the cross-program RQ2 view, each study type was mapped one-to-one onto a question (dose-ranging → what is the dose-response; drug-interaction and special-population → who needs a different dose; food-effect → how is the dose given, since its product is an instruction about taking the dose, not about who takes it; absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME) characterization → how does the body handle the drug, kept separate because it describes disposition rather than prescribing a different dose to anyone; and so on), so that every study of the six fully reconstructed programs falls in exactly one class. Post-approval events — those dated after a program’s first FDA approval, excluding approvals themselves — were classified in the same spirit by what the label change did: moved the therapeutic range, added strengths within it, altered administration, addressed a subpopulation, or clarified wording. Subpopulation events are further split by whether they dose a schizophrenia patient or carry the molecule into another indication. Both mappings are deterministic functions of the extracted vocabularies, applied in 02-analyze/analyze.R; neither re-reads sources. They are single-rater classifications: the mapping is the codebook, and no independent coder recoded it.

Abbreviations in the tables. The cohort table above and the per-program event and study tables below quote regulatory and clinical-pharmacology shorthand: CRL, complete response letter, and NAL, not-approvable letter (the two forms of FDA refusal in this cohort); EOP2, end-of-Phase-2 meeting; MTD, maximum tolerated dose; SAD and MAD, single- and multiple-ascending-dose studies; DDI, drug–drug interaction; TQT, thorough QT study; ddQTc, the placebo-corrected change from baseline in the QT interval, with the trailing letters naming the heart-rate correction used (F = Fridericia); PET, positron emission tomography; ADME, absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion; DDCAR, didesmethyl-cariprazine, the long-half-life active metabolite that governs cariprazine’s accumulation; SPL, the structured product label version published on DailyMed; PMC, a post-marketing commitment; and BID, QD and TID for twice-, once- and three-times-daily dosing.

3.3 Occupancy annotation

Reported target-occupancy values were collected per drug and dose from PET publications and the curated meta-analytic literature (Siafis 2023 for the dose–occupancy–EPS relationship; Leucht 2020 for near-maximal effective doses, ED95). Each approved dose range was annotated against the 65–80% D2 window; partial agonists (brexpiprazole, cariprazine) are annotated separately since they tolerate near-saturating occupancy. No formal model was fit — the annotation layer is descriptive.

4 Results

4.1 The shape of six dose trajectories

The figure below is the study’s central display: the total daily dose range each program tested, by development stage, against what was approved and what stands today.

Tested and approved total daily dose ranges by development stage (program drug only; comparator arms excluded). For the Phase 1–3 stages a bar spans the lowest to highest total daily dose tested in that stage; for Approved (initial) and Current label it spans the labelled dose range, which is a licensing decision rather than a set of doses studied. Xanomeline–trospium doses are the xanomeline component. Phase 1 includes maximum-tolerated-dose escalations; single-dose approvals draw as slivers.

Four patterns stand out.

  • 4 of the 5 reconstructed approved programs lowered their ceiling. Phase 1 ceilings sat 1.3–7.5-fold above the maximum approved at registration (iloperidone 32 vs 24 mg/day; lurasidone 600 vs 80; cariprazine 24 vs 6; lumateperone 126 vs 42). Two cautions on that fold. It is measured against the registration ceiling rather than the current label, which keeps this bullet separate from the re-widening described next. And a Phase 1 ceiling is the highest dose ever given, not the highest dose ever considered for therapy: lurasidone’s 600 mg/day comes from a maximum-tolerated-dose escalation and lumateperone’s 126 mg/day is the deliberately supratherapeutic arm of a thorough-QT study, neither of which was ever a candidate dose. The fold therefore measures how far exploration ran above the label, not how much therapeutic range was discarded.
  • Two programs later climbed back up. Lurasidone’s approved maximum doubled (80 to 160 mg/day (approved 2012-04-26, ~18 months post-launch)); ulotaront’s restart keeps only the top of its range. No new therapeutic dose was ever added below an approved range in this cohort — lumateperone’s 10.5 and 21 mg strengths sit below its 42 mg dose but exist only for CYP3A4 inhibition and hepatic impairment.
  • The index case’s ceiling never moved. Xanomeline–trospium’s Phase 1 ceiling of 250 mg/day is still the label maximum, and it has carried the same 100–250 mg/day titration corridor from Phase 2 to the current label — the range is the schedule. (Its floor did rise once, 30 → 100 mg/day between Phase 1 and Phase 2; the ceiling is what never moved.)
  • The failure case widened at the top, into untested ground. Ulotaront’s controlled Phase 2 tested 50–75 mg/day flexibly; the fixed-dose Phase 3 trials then ran 50–100 mg/day — the 100 mg dose one no Phase 2 study had given. (Both bars in the dose-range figure start at 25 mg/day because each aggregates a long-term flexible study in stable patients that allowed 25 mg — SEP361-202 in Phase 2 and SEP361-303 in Phase 3. The controlled trials’ ranges are the ones quoted here.)

Dosing design of the Phase 2 and Phase 3 studies in the six fully reconstructed programs (count of studies per design; definitions in the Background).

The multiplicity of contrasts across programs and phases in this section is read descriptively — as ranges characterizing the class, not as tests.

4.2 What each study was run to answer (RQ2)

Classifying every study of the six fully reconstructed programs by the dose-related question it answered gives the cohort’s answer to RQ2 in one view.

The dose-related question each study was run to answer, across the six fully reconstructed programs. One question per study, assigned from its study type; bars are counts, the annotation also gives total enrolment. Enrolment counts subjects, not patients: the who-needs-a-different-dose class is mostly healthy-volunteer and organ-impairment studies, and only 8 of its 35 studies enrol schizophrenia patients. Enrolment is also under-counted for the early-phase classes (not stated in FDA reviews for 55 of 194 studies, 51 of them Phase 1), so every total is a lower bound and should be compared within, not across, phase profiles.

The asymmetry is the finding. Of the 194 studies, a total of 35 asked who needs a different dose — drug-interaction and special-population studies — and a further 10 asked how the dose is given (food effect). Only 13 asked what the dose-response relationship is, 8 of them in Phase 2. The dose-response studies enrolled more subjects: 2,035 in the 10 of 13 that report enrolment, against at least 518 in 17 of the 35 dose-adjustment studies. That follows from phase rather than contradicting the count: the dose-response studies are mostly Phase 2 patient trials, while the dose-adjustment studies are all Phase 1 and mostly in healthy volunteers. Subject numbers and question frequency measure different things, and the count is the quantity reported here. Dose-adjustment questions are individually cheap, regulatorily obligatory, and answerable in healthy volunteers. The dose-response question is expensive, discretionary, and answerable only in patients. The cohort’s effort follows that cost gradient rather than the question’s importance to the label.

The same asymmetry appears after approval. Of the 25 dated post-approval events across the 5 reconstructed programs that reached approval, 1 changed the approved therapeutic dose range — lurasidone’s 2012 doubling. This denominator counts the reconstructed programs only, not all 8 approved programs in the cohort: the three list-only programs were enumerated but their label changes were never reconstructed, so their label activity is outside these totals. Their adult-schizophrenia dosing has not changed, but that is a statement from the current label rather than a count of events.

Post-approval label activity by the question the change answered, across the 5 fully reconstructed programs that reached approval. “New strengths” are tablet presentations that did not move the approved range. Approvals themselves are excluded (they are not label activity). “Who needs a different dose” is split by scope, because dosing the molecule in another disease is a different claim from adjusting the dose in schizophrenia.

Post-approval label activity is dominated by 12 changes answering who needs a different dose. Only 6 of them adjust the dose for a schizophrenia patient (CYP2D6 poor-metabolizer and hepatic dosing, adolescent dosing, interaction-driven adjustments); the other 6 carry the molecule into a different disease, which is dose work in the label but not in this cohort’s indication. Only 2 changes altered how the dose is given (lumateperone’s food requirement, cariprazine’s interaction-driven frequency change). The dose level itself, once registered, is close to immovable. The one range change in this cohort did not need new trials: the decisive 80-versus-160 mg comparison (lurasidone-S46) had completed in June 2010, four months before the October 2010 approval that capped the range at 80. The eighteen months after approval bought a successful re-argument of data the agency already held, not new data.

4.3.1 Iloperidone

The case where titration was obligatory. Iloperidone’s α1-adrenergic orthostasis requires a week-long up-titration from 1 mg twice daily (BID) — the label itself warns that effectiveness is delayed 1–2 weeks — and QTc prolongation (+9 ms at 12 mg BID) caps the range at 24 mg/day. This is the cohort’s legitimate use of a titrated design: a fixed high-dose arm here would have measured syncope rather than efficacy, so titration protected the trials’ ability to detect an effect at all. The cost is that the range is not separable from the schedule — what “24 mg/day” means is inseparable from the week it takes to reach. The 2008 not-approvable letter is the cohort’s clearest regulatory dose demand: an additional trial plus safety data specifically at 20–24 mg/day. The dose range approved in 2009 (12–24 mg/day) has not moved in 17 years; what has moved is everything around it — a CYP2D6 poor-metabolizer halving (2010), a formalized day-by-day titration table and marketed titration packs (2024–2025), and a 2026 successor molecule (milsaperidone) inheriting the franchise. Notably, no human PET dose–occupancy study of iloperidone was identified — the range was set entirely by tolerability and QT.

Iloperidone — dated dose and schedule changes, colored by the data family behind each change; dashed lines mark the first-in-human anchor (or the earliest dated human-program milestone, labelled as such) and the first FDA approval. 4.3.2 Lurasidone

The regulator-shaped trajectory. At the end-of-Phase-2 meeting the FDA rejected the sponsor’s flexible-dose Phase 3 proposal and required fixed doses — the cohort’s most direct regulatory verdict on flexible dosing. A 20 mg dose was dropped on PET occupancy (51–54.8%, below the window) combined with its Phase 2 efficacy data, not on occupancy alone. Approval (2010) capped the range at 80 mg/day, reading the dose-response as flat above 80 with dose-related akathisia (5.6% at 20 mg rising to 22% at 120 mg) — a cap below the demonstrated efficacy range, since 120 mg had shown efficacy. Eighteen months later the sponsor won the cap back: five short-term studies, including a direct 80-vs-160 comparison, supported doubling the maximum to 160 mg/day (April 2012). The ≥350 kcal food requirement has never moved. The EU label (2014) admits the full 37–148 mg range that the initial US label had cut in half.

4.3.3 Cariprazine

The metabolite-driven trajectory — the strongest pre-approval dose story in the cohort. Cariprazine’s didesmethyl metabolite (DDCAR) has a 2–3 week half-life and accumulates ~25-fold between day 1 and day 14, approaching steady state only at weeks 4–6 — after the acute trials ended. The 2013 complete response letter was explicitly about this: late-emerging akathisia/EPS tracking a poorly characterized metabolite. The 2015 approval then capped the range at 6 mg/day despite efficacy demonstrated up to 9 mg (and Phase 2 run to 12.5 mg, Phase 1b to 24), because 6 mg carried roughly twice the akathisia of 3 mg. The label carries unique kinetic language — “changes in dose will not be fully reflected in plasma for several weeks” — and a Late-Occurring Adverse Reactions warning. The FDA asked for lower or less-frequent maintenance dosing to be evaluated; a dose-reduction relapse-prevention trial was run, but through the end of 2025 no label change has followed — the lower-maintenance-dose question remains open a decade after it was posed.

1 PET receptor occupancy RGH-PK-15 Dose escalation D3 vs D2 occupancy across the full dose range (open-label multiple-dose PET; the ‘fifteenth’ clin-pharm trial, ongoing at NDA cutoff).
1 Food effect RGH-PK-14 Single dose Food effect on the to-be-marketed capsule formulation (bridging to commercial form).
1b First-in-human (SAD/MAD) RGH-MD-01 Dose escalation How high can daily dosing go in patients; multiple-dose PK in patients 1.5-12.5 mg (slightly more than dose-proportional DDCAR; at 12.5 mg/day x27d DDCAR ~3-fold cariprazine exposure, ~70% of total activity).
1b First-in-human (SAD/MAD) RGH-MD-18 Dose escalation Upper-bound multiple-dose tolerability/PK in patients; defined the top of the explored daily-dose range.
1b Thorough QT RGH-MD-02 Forced titration Does cariprazine at therapeutic-to-supratherapeutic exposure (9 and 18 mg/day) prolong QTc? Largest upper 90% CI of ddQTcNi < 10 ms - QT not a constraint on the dose range.
2 Dose-ranging RGH-MD-03 Flexible Proof-of-concept: which flexible dose range (low 1.5-4.5 vs high 6-12 mg/day) is effective and tolerated? Low range statistically significant, high range NOT (LOCF) - FDA called results ‘more borderline’; publication reports no significant differences after multiplicity adjustment. Drove Phase 3 to fixed doses <=9 mg/day.
2b PET receptor occupancy RGH-MD-14 Dose escalation Occupancy at therapeutic doses in patients: >=90% combined D2/D3 occupancy in basal ganglia at 3 mg/day (the D2 component alone is ~79%; see the occupancy table); 76-86% at 1.5 mg/day. The 65-80% window is a D2 threshold, so a pooled D2/D3 value is not read against it - cariprazine is a D2/D3 partial agonist and tolerates near-saturating occupancy.
3 Pivotal efficacy RGH-MD-16 Fixed Are low fixed doses effective (1.5/3/4.5 mg/day)? All three separated from placebo at Week 6; 3 and 4.5 mg effective by Week 1, 1.5 mg by Week 2 - established 1.5 mg as the effective floor of the approved range.
3 Pivotal efficacy RGH-MD-04 Fixed 3 vs 6 mg fixed: both effective; 6 mg effective by Week 1 (3 mg by Week 3) BUT the 6 mg arm had twice the akathisia-related events of the 3 mg arm with late-onset cases through trial end - the pivotal evidence behind the 6 mg/day cap and late-occurring-AE labeling.
3 Pivotal efficacy RGH-MD-05 Flexible Does 6-9 mg/day add benefit over 3-6? Both ranges effective (high range slightly larger effect, faster onset) - efficacy demonstrated up to 9 mg/day, yet the approved max stayed 6 mg/day (cap below demonstrated efficacy).
3 Relapse prevention RGH-MD-06 Forced titration Does cariprazine prevent relapse long-term at 3/6/9 mg/day? Also the resubmission’s key washout dataset: blinded PK sampling up to 14 weeks after randomization to placebo characterized DDCAR decline (>90% decline in ~4 weeks).
3 Pivotal efficacy A002-A4 Fixed Japanese confirmatory efficacy at fixed 3/6/9 mg/day.
3b/4 Maintenance / withdrawal — Fixed PMR 2947-9 / the open question FDA flagged at approval: can a lower dose than the acute-response dose maintain efficacy (lowest effective maintenance dose), and what are long-term dose-related risks (TD, akathisia, EPS, adrenal)? No adult-schizophrenia label change through 12/2025 - question still open.

4.3.4 Lumateperone

The single-dose approval. Lumateperone was developed occupancy-first — PET in patients showed ~39% peak D2 occupancy at the eventual therapeutic dose, far below the 65–80% window — and the program’s dose walk was short: 42 and 84 mg tested in Phase 2 (84 failed), the FDA advised exploring lower doses, and 28 and 14 mg then failed in Phase 3. The result: approval (2019) at exactly one dose, 42 mg once daily with food, “dose titration is not required.” None of its 5 post-approval label changes moved that dose. Two loosened constraints on how it is taken — the food requirement was dropped (December 2021), and 10.5/21 mg strengths were added (April 2022) strictly as CYP3A4-inhibitor and hepatic-impairment doses, below the therapeutic dose but not an extension of it. The remainder carry the molecule into other indications or record maintenance evidence. Six years on, the therapeutic dose remains a point, not a range.

4.3.5 Ulotaront (failure contrast)

The flexible-dose trap, in its cleanest published form. Ulotaront (TAAR1 agonist — no D2 binding, no PET tracer, no occupancy anchor) never ran a fixed-dose dose-ranging study. Its Phase 2 was flexible 50–75 mg/day and positive; on that basis the program went straight to fixed-dose Phase 3: DIAMOND 1 at 50/75 mg and DIAMOND 2 at 75/100 mg — the 100 mg arm being a dose no schizophrenia patient had received in a controlled trial. Both failed (July 2023) amid high placebo response. The epilogue sharpens the lesson: after Sumitomo’s exit, Otsuka restarted Phase 3 in 2025 at fixed 75/100 mg only — dropping the 50 mg dose that anchored the original range — and a 2025 dose-response meta-analysis of the pooled trials located the greatest efficacy at 100 mg, the dose Phase 2 never touched. The flexible design had answered “is it tolerated somewhere in 50–75?” while leaving “where does efficacy sit?” untested.

4.3.6 Xanomeline–trospium (index case)

The transcription case. The newest approval (September 2024) answers the flexible-dosing question by codifying it: the EMERGENT trials titrated xanomeline/trospium 50/20 mg BID → 100/20 mg BID (day 3) → optional 125/30 mg BID (day 8) — forced titration with an optional top step, coded as flexible in the tables here because that last step was a tolerability decision — and the label reproduces that schedule verbatim, including the fasting window (1 h before / 2 h after meals) and a geriatric cap at 100/20. At the end-of-Phase-2 meeting the FDA requested a fixed-dose study; the sponsor declined, and exposure-response analyses later found efficacy flat between the two upper strengths — the dose question was closed by argument, not by a dedicated trial. That argument is worth reading against the distinction drawn in the Background: exposure in a forced-titration trial is generated in part by the escalation decision, so a flat exposure-response relationship there cannot be cleanly separated from titration having equalized response across patients. The conclusion may well be right; the design cannot establish it the way a fixed-dose comparison would. With no muscarinic PET tracer, the dose rationale traces to the legacy Lilly xanomeline Alzheimer’s trials (75–225 mg/day) and tolerability. Four label versions on, nothing about the dosing section has changed.

1 Thorough QT KAR-053 Forced titration Does KarXT prolong QTc at therapeutic exposures, and are xanomeline/trospium PK dose-proportional between 100/20 and 125/30 mg BID?
1 Food effect KAR-055 Single dose Does food change xanomeline/trospium bioavailability (the basis of the label fasting window)?
2 Pivotal efficacy KAR-004 Flexible Does the titrated flexible-dose KarXT regimen (target 125/30 mg BID) beat placebo on PANSS total at week 5 (proof of concept in acute schizophrenia)?
3 Pivotal efficacy KAR-007 Flexible Does the same flexible titration regimen replicate efficacy in a phase 3 acute inpatient population (primary substantial-evidence trial)?
3 Pivotal efficacy KAR-009 Flexible Does the flexible titration regimen replicate efficacy in a second phase 3 trial including non-US sites (Ukraine)?

4.4 Occupancy: the window that stopped mattering

Reported receptor occupancy by dose (each point one reported dose-occupancy estimate), plotted against total daily dose. Point shape gives the receptor: the shaded 65–80% band is a D2 threshold and applies only to the D2 points. The two exceptions are labelled by shape — the 45% brexpiprazole point is 5-HT2A (not D2, so it is not a low D2 occupancy at 4 mg), and the samidorphan point is mu-opioid occupancy in rat. Partial agonists tolerate near-saturating D2 occupancy. Lurasidone’s points are single-dose PET values, as their labels state; the rest are steady-state daily doses.

Current label range vs the 65–80% D2 occupancy window, per program. Occupancy is quoted as each source states it — point estimate with the reported regional range or SD where given — so precision varies with the source, and a value cited elsewhere in this report from the FDA review rather than the publication may carry an extra decimal. The verdict is derived from the point estimates at doses inside the label range only: doses tested below the approved floor cannot license a claim about the approved range. “Top of the range not anchored” means no dose near the label maximum has a reported occupancy value. Partial agonists are not judged against the window at all, since they tolerate near-saturating occupancy.
Program Current label range Reported D2 occupancy, as the source states it Verdict vs the 65–80% D2 window
Asenapine (Saphris) 10–20 mg/day mean 79% at 4.8 mg BID sublingual (9.6 mg/day) · [11C]raclopride · not stated in review Within the window; top of the range not anchored
Brexpiprazole (Rexulti) 2–4 mg/day 64 ± 8% (striatal) at 1 mg/day x 10 days; 80 ± 12% (striatal) at 4 mg/day x 10 days · [11C]-(+)-PHNO · patients with schizophrenia (N=12 across cohorts) Partial agonist — window logic differs
Cariprazine (Vraylar) 1.5–6 mg/day 45% (14-64%) at 1 mg/day; 79% (68-88%) at 3 mg/day; ~100% D2 and D3 at 12 mg/day · [11C]-(+)-PHNO · patients with schizophrenia (3/cohort) Partial agonist — window logic differs
Lumateperone (Caplyta) 42 mg/day 39% (± 12% SD; median 39% (n=6, 1 h scans)) at 42 mg QD x 2 weeks (60 mg ITI-007 tosylate) · [11C]raclopride · patients with schizophrenia (N=10) Far below the window — approved anyway
Lurasidone (Latuda) 40–160 mg/day 42% (41-43% across regions) at 10 mg single dose; 53% (51-55% across regions) at 20 mg single dose; 65% (63-67% across regions) at 40 mg single dose; 80% (77-84% across regions) at 60 mg single dose; 76% (73-79% across regions) at 80 mg single dose; >65% achievable across 80-160 mg/day at 80-160 mg/day repeated dosing · [11C]raclopride, [18F]fallypride · healthy male volunteers (n=4/cohort); patients with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder (N=25) Straddles the window; top of the range not anchored
Olanzapine/Samidorphan (Lybalvi) 5–20 mg/day (olanzapine component) 43-80% (10-20 mg/day: 71-80%) at olanzapine 5-20 mg/day; 83-88% at olanzapine 30-40 mg/day · [11C]raclopride · patients with schizophrenia (N=12 randomized + 3 high-dose); patients with schizophrenia (n=3) Reported as a range only — no point estimate to place
Iloperidone (Fanapt) 12–24 mg/day — Indeterminate — no human dose–occupancy study identified
Ulotaront (terminated) — (terminated, never approved) — Not applicable — non-dopaminergic target, no tracer existed
Xanomeline–trospium (Cobenfy) 100–250 mg/day (xanomeline component) — Not applicable — non-dopaminergic target, no tracer existed

Two limits on reading the figure across drugs. The points pool single-dose peak occupancy in healthy volunteers (lurasidone, [11C]raclopride, four per cohort — hence the non-monotone 60 versus 80 mg values) with steady-state patient values, and the cariprazine and brexpiprazole points come from a D3-preferring tracer ([11C]-(+)-PHNO) whose D2 component is reported separately by region. The window is a guide to the pattern, not a common scale.

The window’s authority declines across the cohort’s fifteen years. Lurasidone used it operationally (a 20 mg dose was dropped at 51–54.8% occupancy, together with its Phase 2 efficacy data). The partial agonists redefined it: cariprazine reached ~100% D2/D3 in a small PET cohort at 12 mg/day — twice its approved maximum — without the acute EPS a full antagonist would produce at that occupancy, while at the approved 3 mg/day it sits at ~79%. Lumateperone was approved at 39% striatal D2 — but that was the design, not a defeat of the tracer: its own PET shows cortical 5-HT2A occupancy above 80% at a dose giving ~12% D2, so 42 mg was chosen against a different receptor. And the two newest mechanisms ran with no occupancy measurement at all: no TAAR1 or M1/M4 tracer existed during development.

The efficacy side tells a similarly unsettled story, though on much weaker evidence. A published spline dose-response meta-analysis (Leucht 2020) reports near-maximal effective doses (ED95) for 3 of the 6 fully reconstructed programs; the other 3 post-date its search window or never reached a dose-response estimate. Where values exist they point in different directions relative to the approved maximum: cariprazine’s ED95 (7.6 mg/day) sits above its 6 mg/day maximum, lurasidone’s (147 mg/day) just below a 160 mg/day maximum whose curve never plateaued, and iloperidone’s (20.1 mg/day) inside its approved 12–24 mg/day range. These are point estimates carried without uncertainty from a single external secondary source, not from the regulatory record this study reconstructs, and cariprazine’s value was read from search extracts of the full text rather than the abstract. They are annotation, not a result of this study. Taken only that far, they support the same reading as the occupancy points: neither the tracer nor the efficacy curve settled these dose ranges on its own.

5 Discussion

Returning to the seed question — what are the considerations for dose selection of a Phase 2 study in a CNS indication, specifically flexible dosing — this cohort offers five answers written in regulatory history.

Flexible dosing defers the dose question; someone eventually pays. Ulotaront is the clean experiment: a positive flexible-dose Phase 2, no dose-ranging, then two failed fixed-dose Phase 3 trials including an untested dose. The 2025 restart — at the top of the range, with the bottom dropped — is the program’s own admission of where the information gap sat.

Regulators know this, and push back at end-of-Phase-2. The two end-of-Phase-2 (EOP2) verdicts in this cohort went opposite ways: lurasidone’s flexible Phase 3 proposal was rejected outright (fixed 40/80/120 imposed), while xanomeline–trospium’s sponsor declined the requested fixed-dose study and prevailed with exposure-response arguments. The difference: KarXT arrived with a forced-titration design where the flexible corridor was the intended label, making the trial-to-label transcription argument available.

Titration is a dose decision expressed as a schedule. Iloperidone’s range is inseparable from its mandatory week-long climb; cariprazine’s “no titration required” label conceals a metabolite that titrates itself over six weeks; xanomeline–trospium’s label is only titration. Where a program’s schedule is doing the dose’s work, a Phase 2 that varies the schedule and not the dose has not tested the dose.

Flexible dosing is the right design when the regimen is the product — and that is a narrow condition. The cohort contains legitimate cases, and they share a feature. Iloperidone had to be titrated: α1-adrenergic orthostasis makes a fixed high-dose arm a syncope study rather than an efficacy study, so forced titration protected the trial’s ability to detect an effect at all. Xanomeline–trospium’s corridor was the intended label, so a trial of the corridor estimated the quantity that would be marketed. In both, the estimand delivered by a flexible design — the effect of this titration strategy — is the estimand the program actually needed. The failure mode is different: using a flexible Phase 2 as a cheap substitute for dose-finding, then treating a positive result as dose selection. A positive flexible Phase 2 licenses the molecule, not the dose, and the record here shows the difference is not academic.

Caps below demonstrated efficacy are common — and asymmetric. Lurasidone (80 vs 120), cariprazine (6 vs 9), and lumateperone (42 as sole survivor) were all approved below or at the bottom of their demonstrated efficacy ranges, trading ceiling for tolerability. Only lurasidone won its range back — and the reason it could is that the 160 mg dose had already been tested in a head-to-head Phase 3 comparison completed before approval. It recovered a dose it had studied and been refused, which took eighteen months of argument but no new trial. The asymmetry matters for Phase 2 planning: a dose that was tested can be re-argued, while a dose never tested has nothing to re-argue from, as cariprazine’s still-open lower-maintenance-dose question shows.

The occupancy anchor is gone; nothing has replaced it. The 65–80% window organized the D2 era’s dose decisions. The cohort’s newest three approvals (lumateperone, olanzapine/samidorphan’s samidorphan component, xanomeline–trospium) and its failure (ulotaront) were all dosed without a usable occupancy target. Phase 2 dose-ranging is again the only place the dose-response question can be answered — which makes deferring it to a flexible design costlier than it was when a PET study could arbitrate.

5.1 What this implies for a Phase 2 design

The cohort does not support a blanket verdict against flexible dosing; it supports a sequencing rule and a design hierarchy.

Randomized parallel fixed-dose is what answers the question. Three or more doses spanning a wide range — including one expected to be too low and one at the tolerability edge — against placebo, analyzed for shape rather than as pairwise comparisons. This is the long-standing regulatory position (ICH E4, which treats parallel fixed-dose designs as the primary source of dose-response information and notes that titration designs confound dose with time and with prognosis), and it is the design the FDA imposed on lurasidone at end-of-Phase-2 (fixed 40/80/120 in place of the sponsor’s flexible proposal), and it is the only design in this cohort that revealed a non-monotone picture: lumateperone’s 84 mg failed above the eventual dose and its 28 and 14 mg failed below, leaving one dose standing. No titration design would have shown that.

When fixed dosing is untenable, randomize the algorithm rather than abandon randomization. A randomized titration design — patients randomized to a titration target or schedule, not to an achieved dose — preserves a valid contrast under tolerability constraints that would make fixed high-dose arms uninformative. It is the design iloperidone’s pharmacology called for and the middle ground the cohort’s flexible Phase 2s skipped.

Treat a positive flexible proof-of-concept as a go decision, not a dose decision. If a flexible design is used for its power advantage on “is there a signal,” the program should budget a fixed-dose dose-ranging study before confirmatory trials. Substituting the former for the latter is precisely the step that preceded this cohort’s one clean failure.

Plan the range you may later want to keep. The asymmetry above is a planning constraint, not a footnote. The cohort’s one recovered dose was recovered because it had been tested and refused, leaving evidence to re-argue; the doses that were simply never given have no such route, and none of them came back. Testing a dose you may not register is therefore cheap insurance against a cap you cannot later lift.

Ask whether an individual optimum exists before designing for one. Where no short-horizon predictor of who needs a higher dose is available — the situation in acute schizophrenia — a titration algorithm cannot deliver individualization and is doing something else: managing tolerability, or deferring a decision. Naming which of the two is intended clarifies whether flexible dosing is the right instrument.

5.2 Limitations

  • Inferential reach is limited by design, and the discussion should be read accordingly. Six programs is a description of a class, not a sample supporting estimation, and two of the six — ulotaront and xanomeline–trospium — were chosen rather than selected by the criterion, because they illustrate the extremes of the flexible-dosing question. The discussion’s first two arguments rest most heavily on exactly those two cases, which is selection on the outcome of interest. The four programs that met the criterion carry the arguments about narrowing, caps below efficacy, and the occupancy anchor; the flexible-dosing arguments should be read as a mechanism illustrated by well-documented cases, not as a rate. The two end-of-Phase-2 verdicts, in particular, are two observations that went opposite ways.
  • The record shows stated rationale. FDA reviews and labels document what regulators and sponsors wrote down; internal decision-making beyond that is invisible, and “driver” assignments inherit that limit.
  • The RQ2 counts are conditional on one classification. Every study is forced into exactly one question by a single deterministic map, written once and not recoded by an independent rater, and 25 post-approval events are classified the same way. Grouping decisions inside that map move the headline directly — separating disposition-characterization and food-effect studies from dose-adjustment ones is what makes the dose-adjustment class 35 studies rather than 60. The ordering is robust to that choice; the exact ratio is not. A residual 23 studies fall in other / unclassified: six lumateperone Phase 1 studies whose identity the FDA review does not describe, six pharmacodynamic-marker studies (pharmaco-EEG, fMRI, REM sleep, gastric emptying, ambulatory blood pressure) that engage the target without posing a dose question, two adjunctive-use trials, and a handful of switching, withdrawal and metabolic studies.
  • Ulotaront’s reconstruction rests on the registry, publications, and press releases — there is no FDA package for a failed program, so its study list is not enumeration-complete (its unregistered Phase 1 studies are known only in aggregate).
  • Study conduct dates for the approved programs’ early studies are sparse: FDA reviews rarely state them, and registry dates were deliberately not used (to keep the companion recall study clean). Event dates — the trajectory backbone — are documented; study-level chronology within phases is approximate.
  • Facts seen only in search snippets (a minority; the per-fact verification level is recorded in the data) carry lower confidence than the majority whose primary document was read in full.

6 Reproducibility

The pipeline is deterministic and runs in four stages: per-program extractions are merged into the canonical tables (01-extract/merge_staging.py, Python) and checked (01-extract/validate.R); derived structures are built (02-analyze/analyze.R); figures, tables and every reported number are assembled into one bundle (03-tlf/build_tlf.R); and this report reads only that bundle (04-report/report.Rmd). No stochastic analysis step exists — label positioning in figures uses a fixed seed (20260813), which is the only random element. Numbers in the prose are inserted from the bundle rather than typed, so text and tables cannot drift apart. All extraction tables, the data dictionary, and stage scripts are version-controlled; the extraction data model and pre-specified cohort/criterion definitions were fixed before extraction began.

The environment record below is the session that rendered this document. It is not a union across the pipeline: the upstream stage scripts additionally attach readr and tidyr, which do not appear here because the report itself reads only the pre-built bundle. The merge step runs on Python 3 using only the standard library (csv, os, re), so it pins no packages — though the interpreter version is not captured either.
